---
title: "Personalised mass communications: invitations and letters"
---

Another use for Quarto in academic work is producing personalised mass communications, such as invitations to a conference or workshop. You create a template `.qmd` file with placeholder YAML entries for the personalised information and for shared details such as the date. A short R or Python script then loops over a data file (for example a CSV or YAML file) that holds the real information and renders the template once per recipient. The output can be in any format supported by Quarto, such as PDF, Word or HTML.

Because the template and the data both live in your repository, the whole run is
version-controlled and reproducible, which makes it more trustworthy than a
one-off mail merge in a word processor.

## A worked example

The repository [`blenback/wedding-invite`](https://github.com/blenback/wedding-invite)
is a complete, working implementation of this pattern. It happens to produce
wedding invitations as print-ready PDFs, but nothing about the *approach* is
wedding-specific. Swap the template content and it becomes participant letters,
certificates, recruitment letters, or personalised result summaries.

The project boils down to the three ingredients described above:

1. A template: a single `.qmd` whose front matter holds the fields that
   change from one document to the next.
2. A data file: a list of recipients, kept separately from the template.
3. A generator: a small R script that loops over the data, fills in the
   template, and renders one output per recipient.

Let's look at each in turn.

## 1. The template

Everything that varies and everything that is shared lives in the YAML front
matter of a single `.qmd` file. The body of the document is deliberately short,
because the actual layout is handled by a custom output format (more on that
below).

``` yaml
---
title: "Wedding Invitation"
format: invitation-typst
papersize: a5

# Fields shared by every output
couple-name-1: "Bride"
couple-name-2: "Groom"
event-date: "8th of July"
venue: "Farmhouse Wandlitz"
rsvp-url: "https://www.example.com/rsvp"

# The field that changes per recipient
recipient-names:
  - "Gabriella"
  - "Wouter"
---

We warmly invite you to celebrate our wedding with us
```

The important idea here is that the front matter is acting as a set of
**parameters**. For a research use case those same fields might be
`participant-name`, `workshop-title`, `certificate-id`, or `result-figure`.
The mechanism is identical.

## 2. The recipient data

The list of who-gets-what is kept in its own file, `recipients.yaml`, separate
from the template. This is the single source of truth for the run:

``` yaml
english:
  template: "invitation-eng.qmd"
  recipients:
    - names: ["Gabriella", "Wouter"]
    - names: ["Sarah"]
    - names: ["Michael", "Emma"]

german:
  template: "invitation-de.qmd"
  recipients:
    - names: ["Klaus", "Petra"]
    - names: ["Hans"]
```

Two things are worth noticing. First, each recipient entry can hold **one or
several names**, so a single output can be addressed to a household, a pair of
co-authors, or a whole lab. Second, this file is **grouped by language**, with
each group pointing at its own template, which is how the project produces the
same document in English and German from one command. You don't need the grouping if you only work in one language, but it is useful in a multilingual setting.

::: callout-tip
## Keep the data as the source of truth

Because the recipient list is just a data file, you can generate it from
wherever your information already lives: a registration spreadsheet exported to
CSV or YAML, a database query, or the output of an earlier analysis step. You
never edit documents by hand; you edit the list and re-run.
:::

## 3. The generator

A short wrapper script kicks off the whole run:

``` r
source("_extensions/invitation/generate.R")

generate_invitations(
  config_file = "recipients.yaml",
  output_dir  = "_output"
)
```

The `generate_invitations()` function it calls does the real work, and the
logic is short enough to follow completely. For each language group it:

1. reads the template and finds the `recipient-names:` block in its front matter;
2. for every recipient, rewrites that block with the current name(s);
3. writes the personalized copy to a new `.qmd` in the output directory; and
4. renders it to PDF with `quarto::quarto_render()`.

``` r
# (simplified) for each recipient, swap in their name(s) and render
for (i in seq_along(recipients)) {
  recipient_names <- recipients[[i]]$names

  new_content <- c(
    before_section,                           # template up to recipient-names
    generate_recipient_yaml(recipient_names), # this recipient's names
    after_section                             # the rest of the template
  )

  output_path <- file.path(output_dir, filename)
  writeLines(new_content, output_path)

  quarto::quarto_render(
    input         = output_path,
    output_format = "invitation-typst"
  )
}
```

The script also copies the `_extensions/` and `assets/` folders into the output
directory before rendering, so that the custom format and any images resolve
correctly, and it prints a small summary of how many documents succeeded or
failed. Run `Rscript generate_invitations.R` and you get a directory full of
finished PDFs, one per recipient.

::: callout-note
## Templating the front matter vs. Quarto's `params`

Quarto has a built-in [parameters](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/parameters.html)
mechanism (`params:` in the YAML, overridden with `-P` at render time), which is
the natural choice for *computational* reports. This example instead rewrites
the YAML front matter directly as text, because the personalised fields are
consumed by the **Typst format** rather than by code in the document. Both
approaches loop over a data file and render once per row. Pick whichever fits
how your template uses its inputs.
:::

## Key features worth borrowing

Even if you never send an invitation, several ideas from this project are worth
lifting into your own work:

- Treating YAML fields as the inputs to a document (parameterised front
  matter) is what makes batch generation possible.
- The layout comes from a custom output format: a Quarto
  [extension](templates-and-extensions.qmd) (`_extensions/invitation/`) that
  contributes a Typst template. Typst produces print-quality PDFs quickly and
  without a LaTeX installation, which suits certificates, letters, and formal
  documents.
- A `_brand.yml` file holds the colours and fonts, so every output is visually
  consistent and the whole look can be changed in one place. This is what you
  want for institutional or project templates.
- Grouping recipients by language and pointing each group at its own template
  is a simple way to handle several languages at once. It complements the
  package-based approach covered in
  [Multi-lingual Quarto](multi-lingual-outputs.qmd).
- Template, data, and generator all live in Git, so anyone can clone the
  repository and regenerate the entire set on demand.

## Adapting it to research workflows

To repurpose the project, you mainly change the template body and the field
names. Some realistic academic uses:

- Workshop and conference logistics: personalised invitation, joining, or
  acceptance letters generated from the registration list.
- Certificates of attendance or completion, with a name, date, and unique ID
  per participant.
- Study correspondence: recruitment, consent, or debrief letters for each
  participant in a cohort, in their preferred language.
- Personalised reporting: a tailored one-page summary of results sent back to
  each survey respondent, field site, or partner organisation.

::: callout-tip
## Start from the example

The fastest way to start is to clone
[`blenback/wedding-invite`](https://github.com/blenback/wedding-invite), render
a single template with `quarto render invitation-eng.qmd` to see the format
work, then replace the template content and `recipients.yaml` with your own.
:::
